title: Measure a flower
objective: Use observed lengths, angles, and alignments to place one flower or leafy stem more convincingly.

warmup.instructions: Choose a flower or leafy stem that fits comfortably in view. In seven minutes, sketch its main axis and largest masses; check one relative length, one angle, and one alignment against the subject.

explanation: Choose one visible part as a temporary unit: for example, the bloom's width or a leaf's length. Compare it with the visible stem, then check the bloom's tilt and where leaves meet the stem. If you sight with your pencil, keep your arm straight, use one steady viewpoint, and treat the pencil as a comparison tool rather than a ruler.

Block in the largest shapes before adding petals or veins. Then look at the open gaps around and between the bloom, stem, and leaves. As in Lesson 3, a negative shape can show that an edge is too wide, narrow, or misplaced. Flowers differ, so keep the ratios you actually see instead of aiming for a standard flower.

exercise.instructions:
1. Keep the stem and your viewpoint still. Lightly mark the top and bottom of the visible subject, then draw the stem's direction as one simple axis.
2. Use the bloom's width—or one leaf's length—as a temporary unit. Compare it with the visible stem length, then check the relationship once more at the bloom-stem join.
3. Block in the bloom and the few largest leaves. Check their tilt and where they meet the stem; adjust the big shapes before adding detail.
4. Look at the open gaps around and between the forms. Compare their shapes with the page and with each other, as you did in Lesson 3.
5. Refine the most distinctive edges and add only two or three details needed to make your particular flower or stem recognizable. Recheck one measurement before you stop.
exercise.subjectType: flower or leafy stem from life

reflection: Which relationship most changed your drawing: length, angle, or alignment?
Did a gap between forms reveal an edge that needed moving?
Which proportion would you check first from another viewpoint?
extension: From a new viewpoint, compare the same part-to-part relationship on a different flower or leafy stem. Keep the first drawing and note what changes.

teaching.whyItMatters: A few careful comparisons can make a small flower study feel like the particular plant in front of you, even before you draw its details.
teaching.connections: Lesson 3 trained you to notice negative shapes around an object. Here you will compare those gaps alongside the flower's lengths, angles, and alignments; Lesson 2's slow contour looking also helps you see where a leaf actually meets the stem.

deepDive: Comparative measurement makes an impression testable. Compare bloom width with a leaf or stem, choose one as a temporary unit, and mark the estimate lightly. Change units only if a different comparison is easier. When sighting with a pencil, bending your elbow or changing its distance changes the apparent unit. Keep the viewpoint and arm extension fixed; use the pencil to compare, not as a ruler to transfer measurements to the page.

Direction matters as much as length. A slanted bloom-stem junction can make the whole plant feel off if you straighten it from memory. Compare the main axis with the page vertical, and use a leaf tip or bloom center to check alignments. Negative shapes give you another route into the same observation: if a gap looks too thin or its angle differs from the real gap, one of the edges enclosing it needs attention. Revise the block-in before adding small petal marks.

One checked measurement can correct a surprising amount because the parts constrain one another: if the bloom is too broad, the apparent stem length and side gaps also change. Treat sighting as a relative comparison at eye level, not as a way to import perfect geometry into a living subject. Look back often; a leaf or stem may shift between glances.

commonMistakes.mistake: Drawing a remembered, perfectly regular flower instead of the flower you can see.
commonMistakes.lookFor: Petals repeat evenly, the stem becomes straight, or leaves mirror each other even when the subject does not.
